subject: ent
title: Facial nerve and its disorders

steps.tx: The **facial nerve** emerges from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, traverses the internal acoustic meatus, and enters the temporal bone through labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid segments. It gives off the greater superficial petrosal nerve for tears, the stapedial branch for sound dampening, and the chorda tympani for taste. It finally exits the stylomastoid foramen to innervate the facial muscles. Its tight bony canal leaves it vulnerable to edema and temporal fractures.
steps.say: The facial nerve exits the brainstem and travels through a rigid bony canal within the temporal bone before reaching the face. As it passes through labyrinthine, tympanic and vertical segments, it gives off branches for lacrimation, the stapedius reflex and taste. It leaves through the stylomastoid foramen to supply facial expression muscles. Because this canal is unyielding, inflammatory swelling or fractures can rapidly compress the nerve and cause paralysis.

vis.alt: Cutaway of the temporal bone showing the facial nerve emerging from the pons, traversing the facial canal to give off the greater petrosal, stapedial, and chorda tympani branches, and exiting via the stylomastoid foramen.
vis.caption: Intraosseous course and intratemporal branches of the facial nerve.

steps.tx: **Bell palsy** is an acute idiopathic lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial nerve that peaks within seventy-two hours. Reactivation of herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion triggers inflammatory edema, entrapping the nerve in its narrow labyrinthine segment. Oral corticosteroids within three days of onset significantly improve complete recovery. Antivirals provide little added benefit alone. Diligent eye lubrication and night taping prevent exposure keratitis during lagophthalmos.
steps.say: Bell palsy presents as acute unilateral facial weakness that peaks rapidly and affects both the upper and lower face. Viral inflammation causes the nerve to swell within its tight labyrinthine segment, leading to conduction block. Prompt treatment with oral steroids within three days increases the likelihood of complete recovery. While motor function returns, artificial tears by day and protective eye taping at night prevent corneal damage when the eyelids cannot close.

steps.tx: Separating central from peripheral weakness relies on **forehead sparing**, because corticobulbar fibers to the frontalis muscle cross bilaterally. An upper motor neuron stroke preserves forehead movement while paralysing the lower face. Peripheral lesions affect all ipsilateral facial muscles including the brow. Ramsay Hunt syndrome from herpes zoster oticus displays painful external ear vesicles with worse prognosis. Bilateral palsies suggest Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, parotid neoplasms or acute otitis media.
steps.say: Clinical examination separates upper motor neuron from lower motor neuron lesions by checking forehead movement. Because the upper face has bilateral innervation from the cerebral cortex, a hemispheric stroke spares the forehead and only affects the lower face. In contrast, an infranuclear injury involves all facial muscles on that side. Painful ear vesicles indicate Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which has a poorer outcome. Other conditions like Lyme disease, sarcoidosis and parotid tumors require targeted investigation.

vis.caption: Forehead sparing differentiates central (UMN) from peripheral (LMN) facial palsy

steps.tx: Traumatic facial nerve injury frequently complicates **temporal bone fractures**, classified as longitudinal or transverse along the petrous ridge. Longitudinal fractures account for eighty percent of injuries, tearing the tympanic membrane with conductive hearing loss and bleeding, with twenty percent nerve injury. Transverse fractures cross the labyrinth, producing sensorineural deafness, vertigo and facial palsy in half of cases. Immediate paralysis suggests transection needing exploration, whereas delayed weakness reflects swelling that recovers with steroids.
steps.say: Head trauma can injure the facial nerve during temporal bone fractures. Longitudinal fractures run along the petrous bone, causing conductive hearing loss, bleeding and eardrum tears, with a lower rate of nerve palsy. Transverse fractures travel across the otic capsule, destroying inner ear structures to produce sensorineural deafness, vertigo and high rates of facial paralysis. Immediate paralysis suggests nerve transection that may need surgical repair, while delayed weakness reflects swelling that improves with conservative treatment.

steps.tx: Clinical severity is graded using the **House Brackmann** scale from grade one for normal function to grade six for complete paralysis. Incomplete eyelid closure demands immediate corneal protection to prevent ulceration. Incomplete recovery may cause aberrant regeneration, producing synkinesis and crocodile tears where salivary fibers reinnervate the lacrimal gland. Chronic weakness is managed with botulinum toxin for spasms, upper eyelid gold weights, and dynamic surgical muscle transfers.
steps.say: Clinicians assess the severity and recovery of facial paralysis using the House Brackmann grading scale, which ranges from grade one for normal movement to grade six for total flaccidity. Protecting the cornea remains the most critical priority whenever eyelid closure is impaired. During recovery, misdirected nerve fibres can cause synkinesis and crocodile tears during meals. Chronic facial weakness benefits from targeted botulinum toxin injections, surgical insertion of gold weights into the upper lid, and reconstructive transfers.
